I think GrapheneOS is caught between a rock and a hard place, and I think whatever decision they make is going to have huge implications for the project's long-term viability.

On the one hand, Pixel 11 omitting MTE is ridiculous. It was an opportunity for Google to improve the security of its users, security which is now compromised. Yes, they weren't using it on the stock OS, but frankly, they should have implemented it more liberally. Even if Google doesn't care about your privacy, they definitely should be caring about your security and it's not only a bad look, but a real risk to their users when they compromise on a feature like this.

On the other hand, the Motorola partnership is far from guaranteed. Yes, maybe for the first few years it will be great, but anything could happen afterwards and I must say that the track record for companies working with custom ROM devs (in particular Cyanogen with multiple OEMs) has not been great. Like it or not, GrapheneOS is a niche project, and companies aren't incentivized to support niche projects unless it's for something like a government contract or enterprise. It is a huge risk to the project to rest their entire future on Motorola when Motorola could easily end collaboration for future devices in a few years (not to mention, be banned from the US if political tensions with China continue to rise).

Personally, I think GrapheneOS needs to diversify who they're working with and continue development for the Pixel 11. Yes, it's far from ideal, and it would involve a glaring compromise in security. But who's to say that Motorola is going to keep playing ball in a few years? We have yet to see Motorola establish a real track record of working with GrapheneOS, and I think going all-in on this partnership is risky when it has yet to prove itself in the real world. We don't even have a Motorola device that can run GrapheneOS yet!

The way I see it, it's best to provide harm reduction to users and diversify partnerships, and support the Pixel 11. GrapheneOS could state that they strongly recommend Motorola devices and lay out reasons why, but leave the Pixel 11 (and future Pixels) as an option. Samsung won't allow bootloader unlocking in the US and hasn't for years, I wouldn't touch Nothing with a 39-and-a-half-foot pole after the Sunbird incident, leaving Apple and Google as the only real options here besides Motorola.

replies.author: Foggy
replies.text:
GazelleInitial Here these are EL1 registers so we aren't allowed to read the real hardware registers from userspace. What the kernel does is intercept the illegal instruction trap generated and pass through the values it alone is allowed to read. You would have to check the kernel source to confirm it isn't interfering with the values on the way through, but the values shown here seem to match up with what we expect the hardware to return.

It is also possible for there to be 'chicken bits' which allow firmware or sometimes the kernel to disable hardware features in early boot ('chicken' in the sense of the chip designers worrying a feature won't work and have a way to 'chicken out' by turning it off in software). We don't know the situation here: eg perhaps MTE is present but doesn't work, or perhaps they turned it off in this version of the firmware but could turn it on in another. We don't know about that, but there's nothing we can do about it at this point.

(To clarify, I have no inside knowledge and not speaking for the GOS project)

replies.author: GrapheneOS
replies.text:
AtmosphericIgnition They're clearly feeding your statements into an LLM asking it to come up with excuses. Post-quantum secure encryption for verified boot makes no practical difference in the present. There's a slim chance of it ever mattering before the 7 years of support are over at which point it will have been useless. If there end up being usable quantum computers for breaking encryption, verified boot truly doesn't matter with how screwed up things are going to be. Moving to post-quantum secure encryption for verified boot is sensible and it was important to do it at some point but it is not a compelling feature with any real world advantages. It's hedging against future quantum computers able to break RSA 4096 which likely won't exist in the support lifetime of the Pixel 11. Verified boot does not overlap with what MTE defends against and PQC for it isn't relevant to MTE.

MTE is an incredibly useful feature for protecting against the vast majority of remote exploits and the majority of local privilege escalation exploits. It's one of the few strong defenses available in the upstream Linux kernel for defending itself. We plan to make a better implementation and much more integration for it along with many other improvements. replies.text:
Google Support confirms hardware MTE in Tensor G6, currently disabled in public software

I contacted Google Support regarding ARM Memory Tagging Extension (MTE) on the Pixel 11 Pro.

I specifically asked whether the Tensor G6 physically implements MTE and whether it is currently disabled in software.

Me:

Can you confirm that the Pixel 11 Pro has a hardware implementation of ARM Memory Tagging Extension (MTE) in the Tensor G6, and that the functionality is currently only disabled or unavailable in the current software?

Google Support:

“I can confirm that the Tensor G6 chip in the Pixel 11 Pro contains hardware support for MTE, although its availability depends on the current software configuration.”

I then asked whether Google plans to activate MTE through a software/firmware update and specifically clarified that I meant making ARM MTE available to the OS at the CPU/kernel level, rather than simply adding a Developer Options setting.

Google Support:

“For testing or debugging, the MTE function can be enabled globally under Settings > System > Developer options > Memory Tagging Extension, which will restart the device in MTE mode.”

I pointed out that this option is not present on my Pixel 11 Pro and that:

adb shell grep mte /proc/cpuinfo

does not show MTE.

I then asked whether MTE is currently disabled by the Pixel 11 Pro software/firmware rather than being physically absent from the hardware.

Google Support initially recommended submitting feedback through the device so that engineers could potentially address the issue with an OTA update.

I asked again for a direct confirmation that MTE is physically present and only disabled in software.

Google Support:

“Yes, the hardware capability is physically present in the Tensor G6, however it is currently not active in the public version of the software.”

I then asked whether an update will unlock/enable the feature.

Google Support:

“I am currently unable to provide a specific timeframe for unlocking MTE, however submitting feedback helps our team determine priorities for this feature.”

They also stated that Pixel updates are released almost monthly.

Summary

According to Google Support:

• Tensor G6 physically contains hardware support for ARM MTE.

• MTE is currently not active in the public Pixel 11 Pro software.

• The current software configuration is therefore preventing MTE from being available.

• Google Support could not confirm when MTE will be enabled.

• They suggested submitting feedback to Google regarding enabling the feature.

I am posting this because the current GrapheneOS discussion indicates that the Pixel 11 may lack MTE and may potentially be skipped. I thought this direct statement from Google Support regarding the Tensor G6 hardware implementation might be relevant to the discussion.

replies.author: Foggy
replies.text:
[unknown] MTE doesn't need an extra memory chip for storing tags - using a part of the existing memory is fine. So you only pay a 3.125% memory cost for the pages you want to store tags. Effectively you can partition physical address space into one part for data and one part for tags, storing both in the same DRAM chip.

TBI refers to the portions of pointers that are used. ie, roughly speaking each 128 bit memory word gets one of 16 colors (the 4 bit tag). Then each pointer gets one of 16 colors on 4 upper bits by using TBI. If you try to use a pointer of one color to access a memory location with a different color then you get an exception.

For sure it's not perfect, but other mechanisms that leverage a few bits per pointer, e.g., PAC, are imperfect too. CHERI would probably be substantially more powerful, but might cost more in hardware, and deployment effort would be nontrivial. In the absence of a free powerful technique, instead we have tradeoffs.

With respect to MTE, I think as long as code keeps getting MTE trips it means that people are still shipping vulnerabilities, that are each fairly likely exploitable. I think the GrapheneOS team has needed to exclude various vendor blobs from MTE because they trip, and there are plenty of forum posts about commercial apps tripping. To me that does not sound like we have entered a world where MTE is a waste of (fairly modest) resources.

replies.text: Quettaraka That's the right choice since even if we added Pixel 11 support, it won't be as good. It will likely end up being slower and with worse battery life in addition to being less secure. We wouldn't want to entirely lose the security benefits of memory tagging so we'd need to consider using HWASan in the kernel and elsewhere which has 2x CPU overhead. HWASan could provide the benefits of MTE at great cost for certain parts of the OS but unlike MTE, it cannot be used for code we don't build ourselves including user installed apps and userspace driver/HAL code since AOSP removed that code for Pixels in Android 16.
